The latest stable Rust release is **1.99.1** (October 15, 2026), a point release fixing regressions. It addresses:

- **Missing `wcslen` symbol** on UEFI and embedded targets – now included in compiler-builtins as a fallback ([source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html)).
- **FFI `bool` miscompilation** on x86_64 – return values are now zero-extended as the ABI requires ([source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html)).
- **`rust-lld` on macOS** – now built with an `rpath` entry for `libLLVM.dylib` so it loads correctly ([source](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/10/15/Rust-1.99.1/)).

Prior to this, **Rust 1.99.0** (October 1, 2026) introduced bigger features: stabilizing C-variadic function definitions (`extern "C" fn foo(...)`), `#[my_macro] mod foo;` for outlined modules in macros, `IntoIterator` for `Box<[T; N]>`, and several new APIs like `Vec::into_parts` and `String::from_utf8_lossy_owned` ([source](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/10/01/Rust-1.99.0/)).

Rust Release Notes

# § Version 1.99.1 (2026-10-15)

- library: fix missing symbol `wcslen` on UEFI and embedded targets
- rustc: fix miscompilation of FFI `bool` return values on x86_64
- rust-lld: add the rpath for `libLLVM` on macOS

## § Language

- Add allow-by-default `raw_borrows_via_references` lint that checks for references that decay immediately into raw borrows
- Extend `unconditional_panic` lint to function calls that panic when the chunks/windows size is zero
- Stabilize C-variadic function definitions
- Stabilize the ability to use `#[unsafe(naked)]` functions to define C-variadic functions (`#![feature(c_variadic_naked_functions)]`).
- Trait methods are now resolved on an adjusted never type (producing a FCW)
- Coerce from inference variables to trait objects if the inference variable is related via subtyping to a type that is known to be `Sized`
- Stabilize `#[my_macro] mod foo;`. This allows outlined modules (`mod foo;`) anywhere in the body of a custom attribute or derive macro.
- Fix the `overflowing_literals` lint with repeated negation. For instance, it will now no longer lint on `--128_i8`, which is already detected by the `arithmetic_overflow` lint.
- Add POSIX symbols to the `invalid_runtime_symbol_definitions` and `suspicious_runtime_symbol_definitions` lints
- Lint unused `#[path]` attributes on inline modules
- Enable `unreachable_cfg_select_predicates` lint as part of `unused` lint group
- Stabilize passing 128-bit integers via vector registers with `asm!` on x86
- Explicitly document that some allocations are allowed to grow in-place (but none are allowed to shrink)
- We now guarantee that the contents of an `UnsafeCell` can be accessed without going through `get`

- The `invalid_reference_casting` lint was adjusted accordingly
- Account for globally enabled target features in `global_asm!`
- Warn if an invalid `doc` attribute is used on a macro invocation

## § Compiler

- Convert `-Ctarget-cpu` into a target-modifier for AVR, AMDGCN and NVPTX
- Enable `static_position_independent_executables` on all gnu targets
- When providing a suggestion about a missing method, rustc now prefers an exactly matching name from a doc alias attribute over a similarity search from other method names. If your new users sometimes expect a method under a different name, adding a doc alias will now help them find it via rustc suggestions, in addition to helping them find it via rustdoc search: When suggesting method names, prefer exact doc aliases over similar names

## § Platform Support

- Promote `riscv64-unknown-linux-musl` to Tier 2 with host tools

Refer to Rust’s platform support page for more information on Rust’s tiered platform support.

## § Libraries

- Iteration on `RangeInclusive` (`a..=b` ranges) is now optimized better in some circumstances. As a side effect of this, the behavior of `RangeInclusive` values that has already been exhausted (as an iterator) has changed. For example, the return values of `start()` and `end()` on such ranges may return different values, and using such ranges as slice indexes may have different behavior. These behaviors were not guaranteed to be stable, so these changes are considered to not be breaking changes.
- Relax `transmute_copy` to accept `?Sized` types
- Update `transmute_copy` to use a non-unwinding panic
- Don’t escape U+FF9E and U+FF9F in `escape_debug_ext`
- Re-export `core::fmt::NumBuffer` in `alloc` (and `std`)

## § Stabilized APIs

- `IntoIterator` for `Box<[T; N]>`
- `IntoIterator` for `&Box<[T; N]>`
- `IntoIterator` for `&mut Box<[T; N]>`
- `VecDeque::retain_back`
- `core::ffi::VaList`
- `Box::into_non_null`
- `Box::from_non_null`
- `Vec::into_parts`
- `Vec::from_parts`
- `core::mem::size_of_val_raw`
- `core::mem::align_of_val_raw`
- `core::alloc::Layout::for_value_raw`
- `String::from_utf8_lossy_owned`
- `string::FromUtf8Error::into_utf8_lossy`
- `FusedIterator for StepBy `
- `std::fs::set_times`
- `std::fs::set_times_nofollow`

## § Cargo

- Add a new built-in profile `debug`. This is a preparation for transitioning the `dev` profile away from debugging to give a saner default for faster development iterations. Currently there is no difference between `dev` and `debug` profiles. docs#17214
- Workspace members on edition 2024 or later can now override an inherited workspace dependency’s `default-features` field. For example, `serde = { workspace = true, default-features = false }` now turns off default features even when the workspace definition enables them. On earlier editions, `default-features = false` is ignored with a warning. (RFC 3945) #17126

## § Rustdoc

- Add new `unused_footnote_definition` rustdoc lint
- Smarter filtering of trait impls yields performance improvements of 20% on average and up to 40% on some real-world crates. (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

## § Compatibility Notes

- Fully deprecate the legacy integral modules. For example, `std::i32::MAX` should be accessed via `i32::MAX` instead.
- Upgrade `no_mangle_generic_items` into hard error
- The `Pin::new_unchecked` has had its safety invariants changed slightly
- Do not promote references to extern statics
- Ensure that the inferred types of `let` patterns typecheck
- hermit/fs: Return `unsupported()` instead of `from_raw_os_error(22)`
- Fixed a bug where `#[repr(simd)]` was accidentally allowed on macro invocations on stable Rust
- Abort const-eval when there are generics in the type of the value being produced
- Attributes not applying to anything are now an error in code blocks in doc comments
- `Box::leak`: tell people to avoid unleaking
- PowerPC inline ASM: Fix scalar floats being in the wrong vector lane on little endian
- Do not take `doc(cfg())` into account when filtering doctests
- Infer anonymous lifetimes in the types of associated consts as `'static`
- Macros that expand to a semicolon now produce a warning lint (`semicolon_in_expressions_from_non_local_macros`) even when the macro comes from another crate. Previously, such warnings only appeared for macros from the same crate, to avoid showing warnings that can’t be fixed locally; however, this masked problems, as integration tests from the crate providing the macro get compiled as a separate crate, so tests often wouldn’t reveal this issue. If you encounter a lint like this, please make sure to report it to the crate providing the macro so they can fix it; don’t just silence it in your own crate. 

- `semicolon_in_expressions_from_macros`: Lint on non-local macros too
- Split non-local `semicolon_in_expressions_from_macros` into a separate lint
- In Cargo, incremental compilation is now disabled by default when running in CI. CI is detected via the `CI` environment variable. #17220
- The Rust Reference no longer recommends using a single pattern to match a union alongside another value, such as in a manually-written tagged union. This was because it was found that such code would, in some circumstances, result in the compiler reading the contents of the union before checking if the rest of the scrutinee matches the rest of the pattern. This can cause undefined behavior in code similar to what the reference previously recommended.

## § Internal Changes

These changes do not affect any public interfaces of Rust, but they represent significant improvements to the performance or internals of rustc and related tools.

- Update to LLVM 23

## Announcing Rust 1.99.1

Oct. 15, 2026 · The Rust Release Team 

The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.99.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software.

If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.99.1 is as easy as:

```
rustup update stable
```

If you don't have it already, you can get `rustup` from the appropriate page on our website.

## What's in 1.99.1

Rust 1.99.1 fixes the following regressions from prior releases:

- Missing symbol `wcslen`: Some Rust targets were getting link errors for missing `wcslen`, and that function is now present in Rust's compiler-builtins library as a fallback.

The LLVM `loop-idiom-wcslen` pass may introduce calls to `wcslen` as an optimization, and some Rust targets did not have that function readily available in `libc` or elsewhere. The UEFI targets in particular were broken for any project using `std`, as some of these calls were introduced in the precompiled standard library, but the issue was also reproducible for similar user code patterns.
- Miscompilation of FFI `bool` return values on x86_64: Rust functions returning `bool` through FFI could leave bits 1-7 of the return register unspecified, causing callers to observe raw values other than `0` or `1`. This return type is now marked for zero-extension again, as required by the ABI.
- `rust-lld` failed to load `libLLVM` on macOS: This linker could fail to run if the compiler was invoked without the `rustup` proxy, as there was no direct setting for the appropriate library search path. Now `rust-lld` is built with an `rpath` entry for the directory containing `libLLVM.dylib`.

### extern "C" variadics

Rust 1.99.0 stabilizes defining C-ABI variadic functions with "C" and "C-unwind" ABIs. Variadic functions defined this way use a variable argument list (`...`) and accept an arbitrary number of arguments. Rust could already call externally-defined variadic functions (e.g., `libc::printf`). With Rust 1.99, these functions can now be written in Rust itself:

...

The type of `...` is `VaList`, which is ABI-compatible with the C `va_list` type across targets. What types can be read from a `VaList` is guarded by the `VaArgSafe` trait.
